title: Experiences of adult social care complaint processes
official: Complaining about complaints: an exploration of family carers’ experiences of raising complaints with local authority adult social care departments in relation to adults with learning disabilities
summary:
Background and study aims
This project looks at the experiences of family carers of adults with learning disabilities who make a complaint to their local council adult social care department. We want to understand how family carers and local council staff experience the complaint process and make new resources to share what we have found out with local councils and the wider public.
We know that family carers often find it difficult to make a complaint to adult social care, and they want professionals to understand what it is like for them. However, there is little research about their experiences of making complaints or how social care staff think about and respond to complaints.

Who can participate?
Family carers of adults with learning disabilities can participate if they have experience of making a formal complaint related to their relatives care, to their relative's local authority adult social care team. 
Local authority staff who have experience of managing, handling or responding to adult social care complaints can also take part. 
While participants do not have to live in England, their experience must relate to English local authorities. 

What does the study involve?
The project will last 22 months. It has four parts which have been designed after talking with family carers, family carer groups, and council staff.
1. We will read what has been written about adult social care complaints and write a summary of this. (A rapid scoping review)
2. We will talk to 20 family carers of adults with learning disabilities who have complained to their local council adult social care department. We will meet each family carer twice. In the first meeting the person will be asked to talk about their experience of making a complaint. In the second meeting the researcher will ask more detailed questions. The researcher and family carer will make a timeline of the family carer’s experience of complaining. The researchers will then carefully read and think about what family carers said and their timelines.
3. We will hold 3 focus groups with 20 local council staff who have experience dealing with adult social care complaints to find out what they think about complaints and how they respond to them. If people do not wish to take part in a focus group, they can take part in a 1:1 interview. 
4. We will bring together key people involved in the research, including family carers and local council staff in 
three co-production workshops:
Workshop 1 will look at what we found out in parts 1-3. We will talk about this and, together, choose the most important points.
Workshops 2 and 3 will focus on making resources for local council staff and social work students so they can understand the experience of family carers making a complaint. An artist will work with us and help make sure the resources are clear and easy to understand.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Risks: Complaints can be a sensitive topic, and participants sharing their experiences may be challenging. The research team understands this and is experienced in working with people on difficult topics. Participants are not expected to share anything they are uncomfortable with, and they will be welcome to take breaks during the interview or stop and/or continue on a different day. Participants will also need to dedicate some time to take part in the research. However, interviews will be at a time that suits the individual participant and can be online or in-person depending on what works best for the participant. 
Benefits: People who take part in similar interviews often say they find it rewarding and value having the space to share their experiences. Family carer participants will receive £25 per interview as a thank you for their time, and there will be an additional payment for those who take part in the coproduction workshops. Participants will contribute to increasing our knowledge on this topic, with findings and resources produced through the project intended to improve understanding and improve the way local authorities work with family carers regarding complaints. 

Where is the study run from?
Manchester Metropolitan University (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
March 2026 to August 2027 

Who is funding the study?
The National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Research Programme for Social Care (RPSC) (UK)

Who is the main contact?
Dr Francesca Ribenfors, f.ribenfors@mmu.ac.uk

interventions.name:
For family carer participants: 
Data will be generated through individual interviews in a three-step process: 
1. Narrative interview: participants will share their experiences of raising complaints with minimal researcher direction. A broad opening question will be used to initiate the conversation

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Family carers of adults with learning disabilities:
1. Currently be a carer of an adult with learning disabilities (age 18 years and over) or have cared for an adult with learning disabilities over the last 5 years
2. Be related to the person they care for
3. Have experience of making at least one complaint to their relative’s local authority adult social care department with the 
complaint relating to the care of their relative
4. The local authority they complained to is in England

Local authority staff:
To participate in this study, a person must:
1. Be currently employed by an English local authority and have experience of handling, managing or being involved in adult social care complaints, or
2. Have previously been employed by an English local authority (within the last 5 years) and have experience of handling, managing or being involved in adult social care complaints
Exclusion criteria:
Family carers of adults with learning disabilities (20 participants):
People will be excluded from this study if:
1. The person they care for is not aged 18 or over
2. The person they care for does not have a learning disability 
3. The local authority they complained to is not in England. 

Local authority staff (15 participants):
People will be excluded from this study if:
1. They do not have experience of adult social care complaints
2. They are not employed, or recently employed (within the last 5 years) by a local authority 
3. The local authority they work/ed for is not in England.
